sources.excerpt: Friedman Amplification Unveils the Fuzz Fiend and Motor City Drive: Dual-Pedal Breakthroughs in High-Gain Tone Sculpting | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Friedman Amplification Unveils the Fuzz Fiend and Motor City Drive: Dual-Pedal Breakthroughs in High-Gain Tone Sculpting By Liam Carter July 14, 2026 Friedman Amplification has officially entered the high-performance stompbox arena with the simultaneous launch of two meticulously engineered analog pedals: the Fuzz Fiend and the Motor City Drive. Unlike typical product rollouts, these units aren’t rehashes or simplified versions of existing amp circuits — they represent a deliberate expansion of Friedman’s tonal philosophy into the pedal domain, grounded in decades of amplifier design experience and real-world artist collaboration. The Fuzz Fiend delivers a dynamically responsive, touch-sensitive fuzz with selectable silicon or germanium transistor stages and continuous bias modulation, while the Motor City Drive channels the aggressive yet articulate midrange punch heard on classic Detroit rock recordings — think MC5, Ted Nugent, and early Alice Cooper — via a proprietary clipping architecture and resonant EQ shaping. Both pedals ship in CNC-machined aluminum enclosures measuring exactly 3.875 inches wide × 2.25 inches deep × 1.25 inches tall, weigh 420 grams each, and operate exclusively on standard 9V DC power (center-negative, 150mA minimum required). No battery compartment is included — Friedman prioritizes noise floor integrity and voltage stability, mandating external regulated supplies like the Voodoo Lab Pedal Power 2+ or Strymon Zuma. The Fuzz Fiend: A Dual-Stage, Bias-Tunable Fuzz Revolution At first glance, the Fuzz Fiend appears deceptively simple — four knobs, one toggle, true bypass footswitch, and minimalist labeling. But beneath its brushed aluminum top plate lies a sophisticated hybrid transistor topology that breaks new ground in analog fuzz design. Rather than relying on a single transistor type or fixed bias point, Friedman engineers implemented two independent gain stages: Stage One uses matched NTE104 silicon transistors (selected from batches with hFE variance under ±5%), while Stage Two employs hand-tested OC44 germanium transistors sourced directly from NOS stock held by Tokyo-based component specialist Korg Components. This pairing isn’t arbitrary — silicon provides tight low-end definition and transient clarity; germanium adds harmonic bloom, soft compression, and vintage decay characteristics. Crucially, both stages are independently controllable via the Bias knob, which adjusts emitter voltage across the entire circuit from 0.15V to 2.8V DC in precise 0.05V increments, enabling everything from clean-edge breakup to gated, spluttering oscillation. Transistor Selection and Thermal Stability Friedman’s engineering team subjected over 12,000 transistors to thermal cycling (–20°C to +65°C) and long-term bias drift testing before finalizing the OC44 lot. Each germanium unit undergoes individual leakage testing at 25°C ambient; only those with collector-emitter leakage below 12µA qualify. Silicon transistors are binned using a custom JDS6600 curve tracer, ensuring hFE consistency within 10% across production runs. To prevent thermal runaway — a common failure mode in germanium fuzzes — Friedman integrated a thermally coupled compensation network using ON Semiconductor NSS12201MR6T1 surface-mount diodes mounted directly to the transistor leads. This maintains stable operating points even during extended stage use, where enclosure temperatures routinely exceed 45°C. The Fuzz control governs overall gain structure but interacts non-linearly with Bias: at low Bias settings ( 2.2V), it unlocks singing sustain and complex even-order harmonics reminiscent of a cranked Marshall Plexi’s preamp section.
